subject: iceCreamTruck
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: ice cream truck.
Style: Animal Crossing.
reasoning:
I'm picturing an Animal Crossing-style ice cream truck built from rounded, pastel primitives, and deciding to keep it as a simple static model without joints since it's a prop rather than a creature, with parts positioned directly in model space under the root.

Working out proportions now: a chunky van about 5m long, 2.2m wide, 2.9m tall, pastel mint and cream colors, with round headlight "eyes," a giant cone on the roof, an awning-covered serving window, and whitewall tires. I'm laying out the coordinate scheme with the front facing +Z, sketching the cab-and-box silhouette, and starting to block in the chassis and lower bumper as a dark skirt box.

For the rounded body panels, I'm weighing options between a loft through station curves versus importing RoundedBoxGeometry from three's addons, or just building my own rounded rectangle outline and extruding it with a bevel to get the soft, chunky look.

Actually, I realize extruding the truck's side profile outline directly is the cleanest approach — drawing the side silhouette in the z-y plane and extruding it across x gives the whole rounded body in one shape, using the bevel to soften edges.

Still mapping out profile coordinates...

Continuing to plot out the profile points for the hood, windshield, and cab roof, then stepping up to the taller box top with a rounded rear corner, while keeping an eye on edge lengths so corner-smoothing doesn't break on short segments.

Checking that smoothing with quarter-length corner cuts won't overlap between adjacent corners since each only consumes a quarter of the shared edge, so smoothing level 2 should be safe. I'll drop the sharp bumper corner from the main profile and handle the bumper as its own separate part, then move on to figuring out the body's extrusion thickness and bevel.

Since I can't carve windows or wheel arches into the body, I'm planning to fake wheel arches with dark discs or cylinders placed on the side surfaces just outside the body, and I'm checking whether the wheels should sit partly embedded in the body given their position and radius relative to the body's side faces and bottom edge.

Working out the torus geometry and rotation...

Checking wheel arch placement against the body's bottom edge and chassis skirt to make sure the arcs flare correctly without floating in air.

Actually the sliver below the body gets mostly hidden behind the tire, so it's fine, but I could also just lower the body bottom to around y=0.42 and shrink the wheel so the arch sits more naturally as a sill/skirt rather than floating.

For the color scheme, I'm thinking a pastel Animal Crossing palette — cream-white on top, pastel pink on the lower band, maybe teal accents — applied via a paint function that maps position to the outline coordinates.

I want the lower band's edge to have a drippy, icing-like effect using a sine-based bump function along the z-axis for a cute melted look.

Simplifying this: pink icing appears near the roofline using a normal-based check, so upward-facing surfaces near the top get the pink drip effect while the rest stays cream or mint. Now I'm thinking through where the serving window should sit on the box's side.

I'll keep the window and awning as-is, skipping drips near the box side to avoid clutter, and plan for the two sides to differ visually -- a serving window on the left, and a painted cone decal with "SWEET TREATS" text on the right for contrast.

For the cab's windshield, I'm computing the slope plane's normal vector so I can orient a decal correctly on the angled glass surface.

Now I'm working out the side windows for the cab, positioning them along the slanted profile at x=±1.0 with a thin extrude offset outward from the body surface.

Working out the window outline coordinates against the sloped windshield line, insetting the edges slightly so the window sits properly within the cab's angled roofline.

Then I'll handle door details -- a slightly proud panel extrusion, handle capsule, and thin seam lines -- while checking for z-fighting between the side window and the body at their shared plane. Finally I'm sizing the front face for the headlights, which need to fit within the shorter hood-sloped region near the top.

For the headlights themselves, I'm going cute Animal Crossing style: chrome ring eyes with a warm glowing lens and white highlight, a curved smile-shaped grille beneath, and pink blush circles flanking the headlights for extra charm.

Checking proportions, I'm adjusting the headlight position to x=±0.55 radius 0.17 and blush circles to x=±0.85 radius 0.08 so they don't overlap given the bevel geometry near the face edges. I'm also tracing the front face and hood slope curvature to make sure the flat region between y=0.55–1.2 has enough room for these decals.

Actually, I realize I can avoid the addon import risk entirely by building the rounded box via extrusion of a rectangle outline with bevel and corner smoothing, which the SDK supports natively.

Now I'm planning the full scene's part count (aiming for 180-250 parts) and sketching out a color palette with Animal Crossing-style tones like cream, mint, and pink to organize the build before writing the bulk of the code.

Writing body paint logic...

Working out the pink/mint boundaries for hood, windshield, and roof based on height and depth, with drip amounts varying by location, and considering adding small sprinkle details on the roof.

Adding sprinkles via surface scatter...

I'm checking if scatter works on the roof surface with a normal and height filter, then considering adding a giant ice cream cone as a roof-mounted landmark feature.

For the cone, I'm planning a waffle-textured cone with pink and mint scoops plus a cherry, sized to sit on the roof — weighing whether to mount it point-up or point-down with a small pedestal bracket holding the tip, and figuring out the overall height so it doesn't look disproportionate to the truck.

Adding up the cone, scoops, and base pushes the total height to around 4.3m, which is too tall compared to a real ~2.9m ice cream truck, so I'm scaling things down and lowering the box/cab roof heights to bring the overall truck closer to 3.9-4m while keeping the cone ornament charming but not oversized.

Writing waffle texture paint function...

Working out the cone lathe outline points -- tip at the axis, out to the rim, up to a lip edge, then back to the axis, making sure the loop closes properly with the start and end both at x=0.

For the scoops, I'm stacking three spheres (pink, mint, cherry) with a ruffled skirt made from small spheres arranged in a ring around the base of the pink scoop to mimic a frilly edge. The cherry gets a small stem on top, and I'll skip sprinkles or keep them minimal. The whole cone assembly is centered at x=0, z=-0.55, with a sign base planned as a rounded plate on two legs mounted on the roof.

I'm orienting the cone tip-down with the scoops stacked above, held up by a mint pedestal cylinder running from the roof to the tip. I'm also adding a pair of speaker horns on the cab roof near the front, shaped using a lathe profile rotated to face forward along the Z-axis, positioned symmetrically on either side of center.

Still shaping the horn bell with a concave dish face, colored cream-yellow with mounting brackets, placed at roof level near the pink icing drip.

I'm also considering decorative touches like a small bell or bunting pennants strung along the roof edge or awning trim, maybe triangular flags hanging from the cone to the front corners to give it that festive ice-cream-truck charm.

Deciding to skip the bunting idea for simplicity and instead focus on solid core features: the extruded body with paint and bevel, a dark undercarriage box, awning, menu board, serving counter, and a window with a tiny curtain.

Adding chrome front and rear bumpers positioned at the body's bottom edges, then considering whether to add side trim or running boards but deciding to skip most of those in favor of keeping the paint bands do the visual work.

Defining the tire ring profile as a lathe shape with a hollow hub center, then building a white hub cap cylinder with a domed cap for the wheel center.

I need the hub disc to cover the tire's hole opening, so I'll make the white hub radius slightly larger than the inner ring to create a whitewall effect, with a domed pink center cap. Then I'm positioning the wheels: front axle at z=1.55, rear at z=-1.35.

For the wheel geometry itself, each hub is a lathe shape with its axis pointing outward along x, with the tire similarly symmetric so it works on either side by flipping the sign. I'll add the wheel arch details too: a dark half-disc behind the wheel plus a cream/mint half-torus fender arch for that rounded body silhouette.

I'm checking the body panel profile at the wheel positions to make sure the disc doesn't poke through the rounded corners — the front and rear wheel wells need the flat body surface to extend just far enough before the smoothing kicks in. The disc itself is a half-circle shape oriented flat against the side of the car, positioned at the hub height.

For the wheel arch I'm adding a half torus ring just outside the disc, rotated so its flat side faces outward and the tube stays on the top half, keeping the same mint accent color as other trim pieces.

Next I'm moving to cab details — planning a textured windshield plane with a frame outline, plus a couple of thin dark wiper rods laid across it.

Now I'm adding rear-view mirrors made from a capsule-and-box arm on each side, glass-colored side window extrusions with a pale shine decal, and a thin dark swept outline tracing the door seam along the cab's side panel.

Still defining door geometry...

I'm sketching the grille curve beneath the headlights and adjusting headlight placement and radius so the hood rounding and front face proportions line up correctly.

Now I'm planning the serving window on the truck's side: carving an opening into the box with a counter shelf below, then filling it with a dark interior rendered as a textured plane showing a diorama of shelves, ice cream tubs, and a warm interior lamp.

For the window, I'm adding a thick cream/mint frame around the opening, a pink-topped counter shelf protruding outward, and small props like a cone holder, bell, and an "OPEN" sign on the counter. I'm also sketching a striped mint awning to sit above the window.

Building awning stripe geometry...

Dividing into 9 stripes along z, alternating pink and cream for the awning fabric, with mint scallops along the front edge. I'm working out how to approximate the hanging half-circle scallops using half-disc geometries positioned at each stripe edge, facing outward along the awning's front plane.

I'm positioning the scalloped awning piece near the front edge with slight thickness, then considering diagonal support rods, a valance, and whether a menu board could fit in the wall space between the window and the box edge.

I'm sketching out a rounded menu board with an SVG-textured "MENU" panel listing flavors with colored circles and prices, positioned near the cab step. I'm also planning a second decorative element on the rear wall gap — maybe a soft-serve poster or popsicle decal, and considering a hand-painted sticker placement there, while noting the awning width might overlap the menu board slightly.

For the left side exterior, I'm designing a big mural: a cone emblem with "SCOOPS!" banner text, stars, and decorative elements on a large plane facing outward, while also considering adding a small porthole window nearby. I'm working through the orientation math to make sure the mural reads correctly (not mirrored) given the plane's facing direction and up-axis.

Since the body sides are flat, a simple plane works fine for the decal there. For the roof, I'm thinking of adding the cone sign, speakers, bunting, a small rear ladder, a roof vent, and maybe a tiny whirly pennant on the antenna. For the rear, I'll add double doors with dark seams, glass window panes, a license plate, and tail lights.

Now I'm planning the rear face details: door outlines, round porthole windows with rings, red-glowing taillights at the corners, a cream license plate with "SCOOP" text, a small exhaust capsule beneath, and maybe a cute pink heart accent. I'm also considering the cab windshield -- keeping the glass opaque with blue light streaks rather than transparent, possibly hinting at a silhouette inside.

For the headlights, I'm thinking chrome ring lenses with a glowing core, and adding cute details like eyebrows or sleepy eyelid rims above each eye, plus small eyelash spikes for extra charm.

I'm worried the lash cones will sit too buried against the lens face plane to be visible, so I'm weighing whether to bump their radius or just place the lashes directly in the lens SVG drawing instead, extending outward past the circle bounds.

Actually, the cleanest solution is a transparent-background plane texture with the full "cartoon headlight eye" drawn as SVG—lens, glow, highlight, lashes, and eyelid all alpha-cut together, with a chrome bezel lathe placed behind for 3D depth.

For tail lights I'll use a simple glow rounded box in red. Then I'm sketching out the full texture list needed: windshield, side window (glass with shine and seat silhouette), headlight eye, serve interior, menu, side mural, a cone sticker, license plate, and a small pink blush circle—roughly ten SVG textures total, with paint handling things like waffle pattern and hubcaps separately.

I'm going for an Animal Crossing vibe: soft pastels, rounded shapes, nothing too stylized beyond that. Now I'm double-checking the SDK API so I don't make mistakes — static models can skip joints entirely, parts just sit under the root group, and I need to be careful with the part() call signature (geometry, color, options like at, dir, axis, up, rotation, texture, name, flat, scale), making sure textured parts use white as the base color so the texture shows correctly.

I'm also working out how glow() behaves — it needs a single standard material to glow properly, but for textured parts it clones materials per source texture so each colored section can still glow in its own hue. Then I'm setting up small helper functions: a wrapper around b.part for convenience, and a rounded-box helper that builds smooth rectangular shapes using extrusion with corner smoothing and bevels to get that soft, rounded look.

I'm thinking through how the bevel and smoothing parameters interact on thin, elongated shapes — a uniform corner-cut proportional to edge length could create lopsided, overly aggressive chamfers on long thin bars, so I need to adjust the approach for those cases to avoid distorted geometry.

Writing rounded-rect helper function...

I'm making sure each outline has at least three distinct points, then working out how to bevel the rounded box's thickness inward along a quarter circle so the outline still matches the silhouette.

Checking the triangle budget: with roughly 60 rounded boxes needing beveled edges, I need to keep detail settings low enough to stay under a 60k triangle soft limit, so I'll scale bevel steps down based on a detail parameter around 0.6.

Estimating triangle counts for the wall and cap geometry, I land on a low total overall. For a sphere helper function, I'm leaning toward smooth shading for the cute aesthetic even though the spec mentions low-poly facets.

Writing SVG code...

Positioning the ring and lash tips with a bezel radius, then designing the windshield SVG with a blue glass gradient, cream frame, glare bands, and a cute pink scallop banner on top instead of a destination sign; now moving on to sketch the side window shape.

For the side window I'm using an extrude with a painted glass gradient and diagonal highlight stripes based on position, applying the same paint to cab faces and walls. Then I start on the interior SVG with a warm dark background gradient and a cream-lavender back wall panel with shelf lines.

Adding shelf items, string lights, freezer, clock, and soft-serve machine details, then applying a glow of 0.7 to make the interior feel lit from within. Next I'm sketching the menu SVG with a cream paper background, pink border, chalk-style title, and rows of scoop icons with flavor names and prices.

Now I'm designing the mural SVG with a transparent cutout over the cream wall, featuring a big triple-scoop cone, a "SWEET SCOOPS" ribbon banner, and sprinkles, stars, hearts, and clouds. I'm also adding a small popsicle sticker labeled "POPS" at the left rear of the scene.

For the rear plate I'm writing "SCOOP-1" text, and I'm adding a radial pink gradient blush decal plus a heart-shaped taillight glow. For lighting, I'm adding warm glowing bulbs strung along the awning edge instead of a cherry or beacon on the cone sign, aiming for that cozy string-light look.

Now I'm positioning nine small bulb spheres near the wall under the awning shade, and starting to model the roof cone sign's pedestal geometry at the roof center.

Working out the cone sign's layered stack: a mint cylinder pedestal, a cream base plate, a downward-pointed cone body, and an ice cream scoop arrangement on top with pink and mint spheres plus a ruffled skirt of tiny spheres around the rim.

I'm reconsidering the overall proportions since the full stack ran taller than the truck box. I'm scaling everything down — shrinking the cone height and radius, lowering the pedestal, and repositioning the scoops and cherry closer together so the total height stays around 3.95, which feels tall but still cute rather than absurd relative to the box.

Now I'm defining the sign's position and base offset, then setting up the lathe geometry for the cone shape. For the scoops, I'm adding drip lobes using extra spheres and scattering sprinkles across the top surfaces with a filter to keep them on the upward-facing parts. I'm placing speaker horns on either side of the truck, positioned to point forward near the top of the box front.

For bunting, I'm deciding to skip the brackets idea and instead hang string lines with pennants from the sign's top point down to the four roof corners, using sagging curves for a circus-tent look.

Writing pennant triangle extrusions...

I need to keep typing loose but avoid unused imports or parameters since the typechecker will flag them. I'm figuring out the string geometry from the cherry at the top down to the four roof corners, calculating the distances to determine how the pennants should hang along each strand.

For the pennant strings I'm using a slight sag at the midpoint and small pink knob spheres to cap the ends at the rounded roof corners, keeping clear of the speakers below. I'm skipping the rear ladder and adding just a small roof vent before moving on to lighting.

For the vent I'm keeping it minimal with slit grills rather than a full exhaust, deciding it's simpler to skip extra detail there. For wheels I'm adding lug bolts arranged in a ring around the hub using a radial frame.

For lug bolts I'll compute positions directly with trig instead of relying on the ring helper, placing spheres radially around the wheel plane. For the tire I'm shaping the profile with a lathe using a smoothed outline.

I'm also brainstorming extra decorative touches like a hood ornament, antennas, mirrors, door handles, a fuel cap, and whimsical scene details like a bell by the window, a tip jar on the counter, and a hanging chalkboard "OPEN" sign.

For the counter, I'm placing small props—a lathe-turned gold bell, mini cones in a stand, and a glass tip jar with coins—spaced along the counter at specific x/z coordinates, along with sizing out a pink rounded-box counter shelf with its own position and dimensions.

Now I'm working out the window frame geometry: the opening dimensions and center, the interior glass plane position, and the surrounding mint-dark frame bars (top, left, right posts) with their sizes and placements, while checking the gap between the interior plane and the body surface is correct. I'm also considering adding a scalloped pink valance curtain at the top of the window.

Writing scallop valance pieces...

I'm also figuring out the awning geometry -- where it attaches to the wall relative to the window frame height, its outward slope and top edge, and then designing alternating pink/cream striped boxes for the awning, considering whether to keep them blocky or round them out a bit.

Working out the rotated box orientation math...

Working out scallop placement and positioning for the stripe boxes, then figuring out the diagonal support rods connecting the wall to the awning's front edge.

I'm positioning small hanging bulbs near x=1.4, y≈1.98, tucked under the stripe underside so they peek out without stalks for simplicity.

Now I'm moving on to the cab side details for both sides, extruding the window shapes, and adding a pink sun visor slab above the windshield.

Mapping out the body profile coordinates...

Tracing through the 8-point outline, I realize the bottom edge is 4.88m long, and if I apply uniform quarter-length smoothing to all corners, the bottom corners would get a 1.22m chamfer — way too aggressive and asymmetric compared to the vertical edges. I need a different smoothing approach that doesn't scale the corner radius with each edge's full length.

Rather than relying on proportional smoothing, I'll write a manual fillet function that takes a fixed radius: for each corner it computes the unit vectors toward the previous and next points, finds the angle between them, and generates arc points at that consistent radius regardless of edge length.

Setting the remaining corner radii across the hood, windshield, roof, and rear sections, clamped so none exceed 45% of their edge lengths. Then I'm extruding the body outline along the Z axis with a thickness of 2.0 and a bevel of 0.14, checking that the bevel scales down properly when it doesn't fit the full thickness.

The concave corner radius (0.12) is smaller than the bevel (0.14), so the bevel will automatically shrink to fit — I'll set it to 0.12. For wheel arches, I'm placing half-discs at the appropriate body positions, checking the front wheel location against the hood profile height to make sure it clears. I'm also laying out the mural on the right side panel, sizing it around 2.7 wide by 1.3 tall centered at y=1.45, with pink paint drips referencing position along z and y.

Now I'm adjusting the mural placement to avoid overlapping the mint scalloped band at the bottom — moving it up to center y=1.58 with height 1.15 so it spans from about y=1.0 to 2.15, letting the drip just touch the band edge without clashing. I'm also considering adding a small fuel door circle on the rear right, and thinking through the cab door seam placement relative to the hood slope and windshield region.

Working out the window geometry on the cab side using the sloped roofline — computing where the profile boundary intersects at various z and y values to figure out inset points for a trapezoidal window shape that stays safely inside the body outline.

Still working out door seam coordinates...

I'm offsetting the windshield plane along the slope normal and accounting for the fillet radius at the hood-windshield corner, which shrinks the flat glass segment to roughly 0.45-0.55 in length while keeping the width around 1.7.

Now I'm deciding fillet radii for both roof transitions, then setting up the plane's orientation with a direction and up vector for the windshield. Next I'm planning a small pink sun visor as a rounded box tilted forward above the windshield, positioning it to protrude outward.

Placing the visor center slightly above the windshield in pink, then working out wiper rods, side mirrors with arms and bezels near the door hinges, and headlight placement at the front face with a lathe-cut bezel cup.

Designing the chrome ring profile for the headlight bezel and confirming a plane covers the lens radius inside it.

Placing eyes at x=±0.5 to keep them within the bezel bounds, and positioning blush circles at x=±0.8, y=0.78 so they sit below-right of the eyes without overlapping the bezel. Now sketching the smile as a curved path with a few control points across the lower face.

I'm also planning a small heart ornament embedded upright on the front-top of the hood near (0, 1.5, 2.05), with pink fill and a cream rim, giving it slight thickness along z so it reads as a 3D emblem rather than a flat decal.

For the parametric heart shape, I'm using the classic heart curve formula with x and y driven by sine/cosine terms of t, sampled at 14-16 points to keep it smooth without self-intersection, then scaling it to the desired emblem size—this same helper can be reused for hearts elsewhere, like the rear and any mural details.

Now I'm turning to the rear of the car: adding a vertical seam rod between the rear doors, outlining the door shapes as a rounded rectangle at the back face, and placing chrome porthole rings symmetrically on either side.

For the portholes, I'm layering a glass disc inside the chrome ring to simulate reflective shine, then adding small chrome door handles and a low-mounted rounded license plate. For the tail lights, I'm figuring out placement—trying round red lights with a glowing amber ring positioned beneath the doors, near the bumper height, with the plate centered between them.

Working out rear bumper and heart-shaped taillight geometry...

Adding fuel door disc and rear exhaust rod...

Now sizing the undercarriage chassis box to tuck under the body with proper floor clearance, and setting wheel radius so they sit correctly against the ground.

Checking that nothing dips below floor level—the tires with radius .46 should just touch y=0, with axles hidden inside the chassis. With a 14-segment lathe for the tires, the bottom vertex isn't exactly at the pole, leaving a tiny ~0.011 gap, which I'll accept as close enough.

I'm settling on tire radius 0.47, center y 0.455, 16 segments—this keeps the lowest point within an acceptable sink tolerance of the floor either way. For the wheel arch I'll set radius 0.6 at the same center height, and I'm now checking that the wheels sit outside the chassis body without clipping, comparing the chassis half-width against the wheel's outer and inner edges.

I'm narrowing chassis half-width to 0.75 so wheel placement works cleanly. Now I'm defining the body paint function, computing a scallop pattern along the z-axis and determining color bands based on whether a point is on the front face, factoring in the hood's height profile near z=1.

Writing paint logic...

Still shaping drip pattern...

Now I'm adding lighting with ambient occlusion based on surface normal, a warm tint for upward-facing areas, and subtle noise speckling for texture variation before returning the final color.

For the paint functions, I'm defining flat colors for chassis and bumper parts, plus a glass material that creates striped highlight bands using a periodic pattern across the surface. I'm also applying glow effects to textured and flat-colored parts to make them pop visually.

Counting up the parts I need: body, chassis, bumpers, four wheels with tires/hubs/caps/lugs, wheel arches, windows, headlights with bezels and expressions, door details, window frames, awning with scallops and brackets, valance, bulbs, counter props, menu, mural, sticker, roof sign with sprinkles, speakers, bunting, and rear details -- roughly 280 parts total. Time to actually write the code now.

Setting up imports and types...

Finishing the bevel calculation, I'm double-checking edge cases where small radii or thin thicknesses might create degenerate geometry, and deciding to skip the optional name field entirely rather than risk passing undefined.

Writing fillet function...

I need to use explicit coordinate components instead of array spread for the hypot calculation. I'm also checking edge cases: if an angle is nearly collinear (π), the tangent blows up and the control/endpoints collapse to the corner point, which just gets treated as a dropped duplicate—not an issue for my current corner lists, so the quadratic Bezier fillet approach between consecutive corners should work fine with distinct start/end points as long as t stays within the 0.45 min-length bound.

For the body outline, I'm passing coordinates in (z,y) with x fixed, then setting up glow strengths. For sprinkles, I'm defining a capsule geometry and rotating it 90° on Z to lay it flat, then scattering instances across the roof surface filtered by upward-facing normals above a certain height, using a minimum distance and a seeded RNG so they don't overlap or get buried in other meshes—each sprinkle gets stuck onto a hit point with partial embedding and a random spin, colored from a palette.

I'll create fresh geometry instances for each sprinkle rather than reusing one, just to be safe from any mutation issues, and scatter more sprinkles onto the ice cream scoop surfaces using a similar normal-based filter. Now I'm working out the roof sign: a flat cream base plate oriented in the xz-plane, a lathe-generated pedestal shape with a tapered profile, and a cylindrical part to finish the stand.

I'm figuring out the cone's lathe profile and checking height alignment -- noticing the pedestal top actually pokes through the thin cone tip since the cone radius there is too small, so I need to adjust proportions to keep the pedestal hidden inside the cone geometry.

I'll shrink the pedestal to a thin pole radius .035 rising to tip+0.12, staying hidden under the cone's radius .055 there, maybe with a small base ring for stability, and consider adding a couple brace rods from the roof for support.

Now I'm stacking the ice cream scoops: a pink scoop centered around y=3.27 with radius .27, squashed slightly vertically, then a mint scoop above it at y=3.61 with radius .22, skipping a third scoop, and topping it with a cherry around y=3.85, bringing the total height to about 3.95.

I'm placing ruffled rings of small spheres at the base of the pink scoop (y≈3.17, radius .26, 11 spheres, darker pink) and a smaller ruffle at the top of that scoop (y≈3.46-3.5, radius .2, 9 spheres, darker mint) where the mint scoop sits on top. Now I'm computing the angular positions around the skirt ring using cosine and sine to place each sphere at its x/z coordinate.

Now I'm figuring out the cherry on top with a thin curved stem swept with a catmull spline, plus sprinkles on the scoops and heart decorations on the mural and hood. I'm also working out where the bunting strings should attach near the cherry's base at the top of the mint scoop, then run down to the corner points of the sign.

I'm checking that each bunting string's sagging path clears the scoop surfaces as it passes by, computing lateral distances at different heights to make sure the lines don't intersect the scoops' radii. Now I'm planning the pennant flags along the string—spacing six triangles per line and figuring out their size.

Working out the triangle orientation, I decide the hanging edge should align with the tangent direction of the string rather than pure horizontal, then project the "down" direction perpendicular to that tangent so the flag plane stays consistent with the string's slope.

Writing pennant geometry...

Static models can skip joints entirely since geometry attaches through the builder regardless. Now I'm moving on to writing the SVG code, starting with a shared color palette for ink, cream, mint, pink, red, yellow, and chrome tones.

Writing SVG code...

Drafting the windshield shape with a soft gradient fill, diagonal glare highlights, and a scalloped sunstrip along the top edge.

Then for the interior view, I'm sketching a cozy dusk-purple room with a lavender tiled wall, a string-light line with bulbs, and a shelf in cream.

Below that I'm adding colorful ice cream tubs, a chrome-lidded freezer box, a soft-serve machine with a swirled cone, a wall clock, and a cute menu card, plus a soft shadow under the counter for depth. Writing SVG code...

Still composing the cone layout...

Now I'm sketching a second sticker idea: a popsicle with a bitten pink body, mint dip, stick, and ink outlines, possibly with a "POP!" label and badge accent.

I'm also designing a small plate graphic labeled "SCOOP 01" with a heart and mint dots, plus a porthole glass texture using gradients and glare, a soft pink blush circle, and an "OPEN" sign to hang in the window using a plane with short strings for the hanging effect.

For counter props, I'm sketching a lathed gold bell shape and a holder for cone cups using small lathed cones scaled down to sit tip-down in a stand.

I'm also working out a tip jar as a small glass cylinder with golden coin shapes inside and a pink lid, and planning a cream-colored menu board frame with a thin plane for the menu text.

I'm checking the menu board's positioning against the awning and window frame to avoid overlaps, nudging its depth and width slightly so everything fits cleanly against the wall.

Now I'm thinking through smaller details like door handles and mirrored window geometry using a side-sign variable, making sure both sides reuse the same coordinate logic. Writing the final export code...

Structuring the build so deterministic helpers live inside the build function while pure geometry helpers stay at module level, with paint and shading utilities defined for lighting calculations...

Writing body paint logic...

Checking the cab roof and front/rear face boundaries work out with mint below and cream above, and confirming the window glass area stays separate from the paint zones. I'll add a tiny noise multiplier to the shading call for subtle texture variation, keeping tires and hubs as flat paint.

Now I'm writing the glass paint function, computing a diagonal stripe pattern for the windshield highlights blended with a vertical gradient between two blues, then starting the main build function with the builder setup and a seeded random generator.

I'm defining a small `part` helper that wraps `b.part`, adding a typed options interface for direction, axis, rotation, texture, and scale so the calls stay type-safe.

Now I'm building shorthand constructors like `ball` and `plane` on top of it for creating sphere and decal-plane parts with position, scale, and orientation baked in.

Writing cylinder and rod helpers...

Adding tread paint logic...
